v.why: Stepping down from an already large learning rate pulls Adam out of the unstable or diverging regime, as in experiments 7, 10 and 17.
Raising an already large learning rate pushes training into divergence, as in experiment 16.
Smaller batches give noisier gradients, and with a high learning rate they cause instability, as in experiments 22, 27 and 36.
Larger batches give smoother gradients, which stabilize training at high learning rates, as in experiments 30 and 39.
Strong L2 regularization on top of an already large penalty causes underfitting, as in experiments 86, 94 and 98.
Relaxing an over-strong L2 penalty relieves underfitting, as in experiments 85, 90 and 95.
Deeper ReLU nets are more prone to instability at high learning rates, as in experiment 67.
Shallower nets tolerate high learning rates better, as in experiments 17 and 77.
Wider layers amplify the effective update size, which worsens instability at a high learning rate.
Large batches mean fewer updates over 243 epochs, so a larger step size helps and the larger batch keeps it stable.

raw:
These hypotheses come mainly from the 100 experiments plus a prior that Adam diverges at high learning rates. The strongest evidence is for high learning rate interacting with learning-rate, batch-size and depth edits (experiments 7, 10, 16, 17, 22, 27, 36). The alpha edits at high alpha (experiments 85, 86, 90, 94, 98) are also clear. The last three hypotheses (width up at high learning rate, depth up at high learning rate, and learning rate up at high batch size) rest on mixed or thin evidence and are the least certain.
